$comment: What the mock Merchant sells. `cmd/merchant -catalogue` reads it, and selling a product
takes no source change in the merchant: Validate and Catalogue.Search never learn what a
flight is. Where a new one goes has moved since issue #160, and the next paragraph is why.
**Most of it is derived rather than typed**, which is issue #160. Everything after the first
three offers is written by tools/catalogue from a CC0 snapshot of Wikidata committed beside
that program — see tools/catalogue/data/PROVENANCE.md for what was asked for and when. The
generator reaches no network, `make catalogue` runs it, and a person runs that: nothing in CI
and nothing in `make demo` regenerates this file. What keeps it honest instead is a test —
TestTheCommittedCatalogueIsWhatThisProgramProduces re-derives the whole thing under `make
test` and compares — so a hand-edited derived row fails the gate rather than drifting away
from the program that owns it.
**A hand-added row fails it too**, and that is what deriving the file costs. The next
re-derivation would drop an offer this program did not produce, so the test refuses it
first. A sixty-fourth product is therefore a shelf in tools/catalogue/select.go, or an entry
in Heroes if a scripted sentence is meant to find it — and a catalogue this program does not
own, passed to `cmd/merchant -catalogue`, is still just a file somebody wrote.
The first three are the demonstration's own and are copied through character for character.
Their prices, caps and scenario blocks are the beats every diagram of a real transaction
reuses, and the generator carries them out of this file rather than restating them, so a
re-run cannot move one. Everything else exists so that a search narrows rather than exhausts,
a table has rows, and a shop looks like a shop.
A fourth used to stand here: two tickets to a concert, `event:vlado-georgijev-2026-11-14`.
Issue #244 removed it, together with its scripted prompt, because a menu showing the same
kind of purchase twice — this one and the bicycle, both a specific object under a specific
cap — read as padding once the catalogue was down to five sentences rather than the sixty-odd
the shop now holds. See internal/agent/interpret/scenarios.go for what that decision cost:
the one scripted demonstration of a basket size greater than one, and one of two prompts that
buy without waiting.
Nothing above this file was ever the obstacle. `item.attr.<name>` is open by construction —
AGENTS.md: 'core does not know what a flight is and should not have to' — the field registry
names nothing aviation, and Catalogue.Search evaluates constraints against a subject without
knowing what it is selling. Three Go literals were the whole of what stood in the way.
The rules are in merchant.CatalogueFile.Validate and nowhere else. There is deliberately no
JSON Schema beside this file: contracts/ is a model generator, every schema there becomes a Go
type and a TypeScript type, and a catalogue is instances — so `make generate` would emit a type
per product. A schema written here instead, purely to validate, would state the loader's rules
a second time, and the second copy is the one that drifts.
`currency` is one field for the whole file. Per-offer currency would let a `lte 40000 USD` cap
sit against a `38000 EUR` price, and constraint's money comparison refuses a mismatch rather
than converting — so the symptom is not a wrong answer but a prompt that matches nothing, with
no failing test anywhere. Amounts are minor units: 24000 is $240.00.
`merchant` carries no identifier. Who this merchant is has to agree with cmd/merchant, which is
given it on the command line, so a value written here could only ever drift from the binary it
names — the same reason deploy/demo.json does not restate the four role identifiers. 5399 is
miscellaneous general merchandise, which is what a shop selling flights, bicycles and ladders
from one counter would trade under.
An offer carrying `route.origin` and `route.destination` is a flight, and the inventory the
Human Present flow buys through — GET /checkout?from=BEG&to=PMI — quotes that route on that
offer's own prices. **No two offers may describe the same route**, and a file describing none
at all is refused too.
That rule used to be 'exactly one offer may carry them', on the ground that the inventory
quotes one route so two offers would mean choosing, and choosing by iteration order is not a
choice. The premise held and the conclusion was too strong: what the checkout needs is one
answer for the route it names, which a shop selling a dozen departures gives perfectly well as
long as no two of them are the same departure. Issue #160 replaced it, and the ambiguity is
now refused exactly where it is an ambiguity.
The rule is the attributes rather than the category, and that has not moved: 'flights' is a
string whoever wrote this file picked, while those two attribute names are already
load-bearing — the scripted prompt that goes looking for the demonstration's own flight
constrains on both by name. A second offer in category 'flights' is stock; a second offer
describing BEG→PMI is a question with two answers.
`scenario` is the offer declaring what it is for, and it is the part of this file that is not
obvious. `cap` is the bound the prompt going looking for this offer places on the price; `found`
is what that prompt is then supposed to do — `always`, `at-the-last-price`, or `never` for
something the search is meant not to return. Those are the same claims a Go table makes about
the three the demonstration is written around, one row each, and holding them here is what makes
the sixty beside them state one too. A price edited past its cap does not fail to compile, does
not fail to load, and would not fail a test written against three constants a derived product
never acquires: it produces a search box that answers nothing for a prompt the documentation
says works.
All three values are in use since the catalogue was widened. `never` was scenery nothing
claimed — a product the search is meant not to return is what shows a reader that a list of
forty rows was filtered rather than merely short — and tools/catalogue's price.go is where the
proportions are argued.
`image_url` is root-relative and refused at load if it is not, including a protocol-relative
`//host/…`. That argument is older than this file — an image fetched from a host this project
does not control would make a screenshot depend on somebody else's uptime, and would put a
network call one careless test away — but it used to be a comment beside a literal a reviewer
had read. The guard exists because the data moved: an editor is now enough to change it.
The illustrations under /images/catalogue are hand-drawn — three for the offers below, and a
fourth, unused since issue #244 removed the concert offer they were drawn for, that this
generator does not touch and does not delete. Everything under /images/catalogue/derived is a
generated mark — one per offer, a function of the offer's own identifier, in the same frame and
the same seven palette tokens. Sixty pictures do not scale by hand and must not scale by
fetching; a handful of category drawings shared across sixty rows would read as a mock-up of a
shop rather than a shop, and would leave the next shelf needing somebody to draw.
tools/catalogue/mark.go is where that trade is argued.
Every offer moves at least once. Issue #192 is why it started that way and issue #198 is why
only one of them still needs to: a Human Not Present watch attempts on a step change and never
on a price — see agent.Watch — so the ladders, which hold one flat price already inside their
own cap, gave a watch nothing to act on and ran until the open mandate pair's hour expired, a
state about the clock rather than about the purchase.
#198 answered that one level up. That prompt carries no condition — "find and buy telescopic
ladders, cheapest" is an instruction — so the interpreter now says so, and the agent buys at
the opening price rather than waiting for a step. **Its second price is therefore no longer
load-bearing.** It is kept rather than removed, because it is what a browser started before this
frontend learnt to send the trigger still needs, and because moving a price tests and a
screenshot are written against is not worth it to delete a fact nothing now depends on.
Removing it is a decision on its own terms, not a tidy-up.
The three still split unevenly, and what tells them apart is *what the sentence asked* rather
than why the price moves. The flight and the bicycle are conditional — they open outside the
cap their own prompt names and step into it, which is the beat the autonomous flow exists to
show. The ladders are an instruction, and were never outside their cap: nothing is ever refused
on them, and the purchase completes at the first price the merchant quotes.
The bicycle's identifier is named character for character by the scripted constraint sets in
internal/agent/interpret/scenarios.go, because that prompt approves one specific object rather
than a class of object. Nothing enforces the match — core-isolation keeps that package and the
merchant from sharing a table — and the symptom of a divergence is not a failing test but a demo
where the prompt finds nothing. Grep for the identifier before changing either side. The flight
and the ladders are matched on attributes and category instead.
Those three facts are what a wide catalogue must not collide with, and the two matched on
something other than an identifier are the ones a new product could reach by accident. The
ladders sentence sends `item.category eq ladders` and nothing else, and the flight sentence
sends both route codes; the agent then buys the first candidate the merchant returns and asks
nobody — see settle in internal/agent/authorise.go. So a second offer in category `ladders`,
or a second BEG→PMI, does not fail to load and does not fail to search: it changes what the
demonstration buys. tools/catalogue's Reserved is what keeps the generator off them, and
TestEveryScriptedPromptFindsOneCandidate is what measures it through the real query.
